# Building Your First Workflow with Chainlink CRE

The Chainlink CRE (Chainlink Runtime Environment) getting-started tutorial walks you through building your first workflow step by step. Using the CRE SDK (available in Go and TypeScript), you build Workflows. Using the CRE CLI, you compile them into binaries and deploy them to production, where CRE runs them across a Decentralized Oracle Network (DON).

## What the Onchain Calculator Does

The tutorial has you build a project called the **Onchain Calculator**. You will build a simple but powerful "Onchain Calculator" workflow. By the end of the tutorial, your workflow will perform four core actions:

Run on a schedule using the Cron Trigger. Fetch a random number from a public API using the HTTP Capability. Read a value from a smart contract using the EVM Read Capability. Combine the two values and write the final result back to the blockchain using the EVM Write Capability.

In short, it fetches an offchain random number, reads an onchain value, combines them mathematically, and writes the result back onchain. This tutorial is designed to teach you the core features of the CRE SDK in a logical progression. You can use any of the supported languages, Go or TypeScript using the language selector.

## The Build Process, Step by Step

**Prerequisites — Install the CLI:** Download and install the cre command-line tool. You'll also need a CRE account and to be logged in via the CLI, plus a funded Sepolia testnet account.

**Part 1 – Project Setup & Simulation:** Initialize a new, blank CRE project and run your first "Hello World!" simulation. You start from a template — use the arrow keys to select the Hello World example and press Enter, starting from scratch to learn all the configuration steps. The CLI will then create a new onchain-calculator directory and initialize your first workflow within it. The init command creates a directory with a standard structure and generates your first workflow code.

The project structure it generates includes a workflow subfolder (e.g., `my-calculator-workflow/`) with files like `main.ts` (or `main.go`), `config.staging.json`, `workflow.yaml`, plus top-level `.env`, `project.yaml`, and `secrets.yaml` files. You'll configure your environment by setting a private key: the simulator requires a private key to initialize its environment, even for workflows that don't interact with the blockchain yet. This key will be used in later parts to read from and send transactions to the Sepolia testnet — open the .env file located in your onchain-calculator/ directory. Note that your private key must be the 64-character hexadecimal string, without the 0x prefix.

You then run your first simulation. The cre workflow simulate command compiles your workflow and executes it locally. A typical simulation output looks like this: the workflow runs locally, making real calls to configured RPCs and HTTP endpoints, and the simulator displays logs from your workflow and the final execution result.

**Part 2 – Fetching Offchain Data:** In this section, you modify your workflow to fetch data from a public API using the CRE SDK's http.Client. You add an API endpoint to your config file so you can change the URL without editing code. This URL calls the public mathjs.org API and uses its randomInt(min, max) function to return a random integer between 1 and 100. This is the "random number" side of the calculation.

**Part 3 – Reading an Onchain Value:** Here you configure your workflow to read from a smart contract using the EVM Read Capability. This involves specifying a chain selector and an RPC URL. A chain selector is a unique identifier used by Chainlink to specify a blockchain, referenced as a string name in config files (e.g., "ethereum-testnet-sepolia") or as a numeric ID used internally by the SDK. For your workflow to interact with the blockchain, it needs an RPC endpoint.

**Part 4 – Writing Onchain:** This completes the loop by writing the combined result back to a smart contract using the EVM Write Capability. You run the simulation with the `--broadcast` flag to actually send the transaction: run the simulation from your project root (the onchain-calculator/ folder) — because there is only one trigger, the simulator runs it automatically — using cre workflow simulate my-calculator-workflow --target staging-settings --broadcast. The workflow then writes to a consumer contract, and your workflow will show the complete end-to-end execution, including the final log of the result object containing the transaction hash.

You can verify the result onchain: navigate to the CalculatorConsumer contract, expand the latestResult function and click Query — the values should match the finalResult, offchainValue, and onchainValue from your workflow logs.

## The Big Picture

By completing the tutorial, you complete the end-to-end loop: triggering a workflow, fetching data, reading onchain state, and verifiably writing the result back to a public blockchain. This demonstrates CRE's core value: seamlessly combining onchain and offchain operations in a single workflow — reading from blockchains, calling APIs, performing computations, and writing results back onchain.

You can find the full tutorial starting at the [Getting Started: Overview](https://docs.chain.link/cre/getting-started/overview) page in the Chainlink documentation, with a language selector so you can follow along in either Go or TypeScript.

I'd strongly recommend cross-checking against the official docs at **docs.chain.link/cre**, since CRE is evolving quickly.

## What Chainlink CRE is (the mental model to build first)

CRE stands for the **Chainlink Runtime Environment**. Before touching any tutorial, get comfortable with the core idea: a **workflow** is a piece of code that runs on a decentralized network (a DON), reacts to a **trigger** (a schedule/cron, an HTTP request, an onchain event, etc.), uses **capabilities** (like fetching data from an API, or reading/writing onchain), and can then produce a result — often writing something back onchain.

So the conceptual reading order before the tutorial is roughly:
1. **What is CRE / the workflow model** — triggers, capabilities, and the compute-then-write pattern.
2. **Architecture basics** — that your workflow runs across a DON, not on a single server.
3. **SDK choice** — CRE workflows are typically written in Go (and TypeScript is part of the ecosystem); pick the language track the docs point you to.

## Prerequisites to set up before the getting-started tutorial

Based on the docs, the key setup items are environment/account related. You'll need a **CRE account and to be authenticated via the CLI**, and if your workflow writes onchain you configure a private key (e.g. `CRE_ETH_PRIVATE_KEY`) in a `.env` file. Concretely, plan to:

- **Install the CRE CLI** — your main tool for creating, simulating, and deploying workflows.
- **Create a CRE account and log in** with the CLI.
- **Set up your language toolchain** (Go, typically) and a project directory.
- **Configure a `.env`** with a funded test private key *if* you'll be doing onchain writes.
- Have basic wallet/testnet familiarity (a testnet like Sepolia and some test funds).

A nice intermediate step before full deployment is **local simulation** — CRE lets you run a workflow locally to see the final execution result without deploying to a live network, which is great for learning and debugging.

## What you'll end up building

The getting-started flow generally walks you from a minimal workflow up to a working end-to-end one. Expect to build something like a **workflow triggered on a schedule (or by an event) that fetches external data via an HTTP/API capability, processes it in your workflow code, and writes the result to a smart contract onchain** — the CRE equivalent of a "hello world" that demonstrates the full trigger → compute → onchain-write loop. You'll typically first *simulate* it locally, then *deploy* it to the DON and observe it running.

## Suggested step-by-step order

1. Read the **CRE overview / concepts** page.
2. Install the **CLI** and create/authenticate your **account**.
3. Set up your **project and `.env`**.
4. Write a minimal workflow and **simulate it locally**.
5. Follow the **getting-started tutorial** to build and deploy the full data-fetch-and-write workflow.
6. Iterate: add triggers, more capabilities, and onchain interactions.

results.prompt: In Chainlink CRE, which capability does the getting-started tutorial use to fetch data from an external API, and which is used to write a result to the blockchain?
results.answer:
Based on the Chainlink CRE getting-started tutorial (the "Onchain Calculator"), here's the answer:

The tutorial uses two distinct capabilities for these tasks:

**Fetching data from an external API — the HTTP Capability.** The tutorial fetches a random number from a public API using the HTTP Capability. Specifically, in Part 2 you use the http.SendRequest helper to fetch data from the public api.mathjs.org API and integrate the offchain data into your main workflow logic. Under the hood, the HTTP capability is a decentralized service that allows your workflow to securely interact with any external, offchain API, and can be used to both fetch data from and send data to other systems.

**Writing a result to the blockchain — the EVM Write Capability.** The tutorial reads a value from a smart contract using the EVM Read Capability, then combines the two values and writes the final result back to the blockchain using the EVM Write Capability. In Part 4, you modify your workflow to write data to the blockchain using the EVM capability and execute your first onchain write transaction through CRE.

So the complete flow demonstrated is: triggering a workflow, fetching data, reading onchain state, and verifiably writing the result back to a public blockchain — with the **HTTP capability** handling the external API fetch and the **EVM Write capability** handling the onchain write.
